### Libraries
```{r libraries, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(factoextra)
library(cluster)
library(psych)
```

## Data Handling
### Load data
```{r}
df <- read_csv("../data/early_2012_2013_loan_sample_with_outcome.txt")
```

The dataset contains 50,000 loan applications with 57 variables covering borrower demographics, loan characteristics, and repayment outcomes.

### Data overview
```{r}
glimpse(df)
```

### Data preparation
```{r}
df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    loan_is_bad = ifelse(loan_is_bad, 1, 0),
    revol_util = as.numeric(gsub("%", "", revol_util)),
    grade = factor(grade, levels = c("A","B","C","D","E","F","G"), ordered = TRUE)
  )
```

```{r}
sapply(df[, c("loan_is_bad","dti","revol_util","annual_inc","grade")], class)
```

```{r}
df <- df %>%
  drop_na(loan_is_bad, dti, revol_util, annual_inc, grade)
nrow(df)
```

Data type conversion was successful across all five variables.

Missing values of 31 rows were dropped (50,000 → 49,969), indicating the dataset is very clean with less than 0.1% missingness across the five key analysis variables. This is negligible and the removal will not introduce any meaningful bias into the analysis.

# 1. A/B Testing of Loan Review Policies

## 1.1 Policy Definition
Policy A (Conservative): Approve if grade is A/B/C AND dti <= 20 AND annual_inc >= 40000 AND revol_util <= 60.
A strict DTI cap of 20 reflects standard conservative lending practice, limiting exposure to borrowers with high debt burdens. The income floor of £40,000 ensures minimum repayment capacity. Grade A/B/C restricts to borrowers with verified creditworthiness. Revolving utilisation <= 60% screens out borrowers who are heavily reliant on existing credit lines.

Policy B (Moderate): Same criteria but relaxes DTI threshold to 30. 
A DTI of up to 30 is commonly used as the upper boundary in mainstream lending. Relaxing this threshold expands the addressable borrower pool while retaining all other risk controls, allowing assessment of whether the incremental loans are profitable.

### Policy rules
```{r}
df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    approve_A = ifelse(
      grade %in% c("A","B","C") &
      dti <= 20 &
      annual_inc >= 40000 &
      revol_util <= 60, 1, 0),

    approve_B = ifelse(
      grade %in% c("A","B","C") &
      dti <= 30 &
      annual_inc >= 40000 &
      revol_util <= 60, 1, 0)
  )
```

### Approval rate comparison
```{r}
df %>%
  summarise(
  Policy_A = mean(approve_A),
  Policy_B = mean(approve_B),
  Absolute_Difference = Policy_B - Policy_A,
  Percent_Increase = ((Policy_B - Policy_A)/Policy_A)*100
)
```

## 1.2 Evaluation Metric and Hypotheses
Primary metric: Average profit per loan application.

$$\text{Profit}_i = \text{total_pymnt}_i - \text{funded_amnt}_i$$

$$\text{OEC} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \text{approve_policy}_i \times \text{Profit}_i$$
 
H0: The mean profit per application is equal under Policy A and Policy B.

H1: The mean profit per application under Policy B is greater than Policy A.
         
          
The business objective is profitability. False positive rate alone does not capture the magnitude of gains from good loans or losses from defaults.
Average profit per application integrates both dimensions, approval volume and loan outcome into a single comparable figure aligned with business value.

### Profit calculation
```{r}
df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    profit   = total_pymnt - funded_amnt,
    profit_A = approve_A * profit,
    profit_B = approve_B * profit
  )
```

### OEC comparison
```{r}
df %>% summarise(OEC_A = mean(profit_A), OEC_B = mean(profit_B), Diff = OEC_B - OEC_A)
```


## 1.3 Policy Comparison

### Paired t-test
```{r}
test <- t.test(df$profit_B, df$profit_A, paired = TRUE)
test$p.value
test$conf.int
```
The paired t-test produces an extremely small p-value (p < 0.001), providing very strong statistical evidence that the average profit per loan application differs between Policy A and Policy B. Consequently, the null hypothesis of equal mean profitability is rejected. The 95% confidence interval for the mean profit difference ranges from approximately £52.10 to £70.84 per application and is entirely positive, confirming that Policy B generates higher expected profitability. This indicates that the observed improvement is not only statistically significant but also economically meaningful for lending performance.


```{r}
test_one <- t.test(df$profit_B, df$profit_A, paired = TRUE, alternative = "greater")
test_one$p.value
```
The one-sided paired t-test directly evaluates whether Policy B yields higher profit than Policy A. The extremely small p-value (p < 0.001) provides strong evidence in favour of the alternative hypothesis, confirming that Policy B significantly increases average profit per application.

Overall, the statistical analysis consistently indicates that the relaxed lending criteria under Policy B improve profitability at the portfolio level.


### Approval and Default Rate Summary
```{r}
policy_summary <- df %>%
  summarise(
    N            = n(),
    Approval_A   = mean(approve_A),
    Approval_B   = mean(approve_B),
    Approval_Rel_Increase_pct = ((mean(approve_B) - mean(approve_A)) / mean(approve_A)) * 100,
    Default_A    = mean(loan_is_bad[approve_A == 1]),
    Default_B    = mean(loan_is_bad[approve_B == 1])
  )
policy_summary
```
Policy B results in a slightly higher default rate (10.7%) compared with Policy A (9.9%). This increase in risk is expected because Policy B relaxes the debt-to-income threshold, allowing more borrowers to qualify. However, despite the modest increase in defaults, Policy B still generates substantially higher average profit per application.


### Marginal Loan Profit Distribution
```{r}
diff_data <- df %>%
  filter(approve_B != approve_A) %>%
  mutate(diff = profit_B - profit_A)

ggplot(diff_data, aes(diff)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Profit Impact of Loans Approved by Policy B Only",
    x     = "Profit Difference (B - A)",
    y     = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The histogram illustrates the distribution of profit differences for loans that would be approved under Policy B but rejected under Policy A. While some of these additional loans generate losses, many produce positive returns, and several yield substantial profits. This indicates that relaxing the debt-to-income threshold introduces additional risk but also allows profitable opportunities. Overall, the distribution supports the earlier finding that Policy B increases average profit per application despite slightly higher default rates.

## 1.4 Limitations
This analysis is based on observational historical data rather than a randomized experiment. As a result, causal interpretation should be treated with caution. Borrowers were not randomly assigned to the two policies, and the outcomes observed in the dataset may reflect underlying borrower characteristics rather than the policy change itself. 

In addition, the dataset only contains loans that were historically issued, meaning outcomes for borrowers who would have been newly approved under Policy B are uncertain. The profit metric used is also simplified and does not capture all operational costs faced by lenders. Therefore, while the results suggest that Policy B may improve profitability, further testing using a controlled experiment would be necessary before implementation.



# 2.  Borrower Segmentation via Cluster Analysis

## 2.1 Feature Selection and Methodology

### Variable Selection
```{r}
cluster_vars <- c("grade", "annual_inc", "dti", "revol_util")

df2 <- df %>%
  select(all_of(c(cluster_vars, "loan_is_bad", "approve_A", "approve_B"))) %>%
  drop_na()
```
1. grade: LendingClub's internal creditworthiness assessment, encapsulating credit history, payment behaviour, and risk tier.

2. annual_inc: Primary indicator of repayment capacity.

3. dti: Debt-to-income ratio captures existing financial obligations relative to income, a key driver of default risk.

4. revol_util: Revolving credit utilisation reflects liquidity pressure and reliance on credit lines.

These four variables together capture creditworthiness, income capacity, leverage, and credit behaviour, distinct dimensions of borrower risk.

### Feature Engineering
```{r}
df2 <- df2 %>%
  mutate(
    grade_num = as.numeric(
      factor(grade,
             levels = c("A","B","C","D","E","F","G"),
             ordered = TRUE)
    ),
    annual_inc_log = log1p(annual_inc)
  )
```
annual_inc is log-transformed (log1p) due to extreme positive skewness. Without transformation, high-income outliers would dominate Euclidean distances and distort cluster assignments.

grade is converted to an ordered integer (1=A … 7=G) to preserve its ordinal risk ranking in the distance metric.

### Select Clustering Variables
```{r}
df_clust <- df2 %>%
  select(grade_num, annual_inc_log, dti, revol_util)
```

### Mahalanobis Distance for Outlier Detection
```{r}
Maha      <- mahalanobis(df_clust, colMeans(df_clust), cov(df_clust))
k_vars    <- ncol(df_clust) 
MahaPvalue <- pchisq(Maha, df = k_vars, lower.tail = FALSE)
cat("Number of outliers (p < 0.001):", sum(MahaPvalue < 0.001), "\n")
```
Mahalanobis distance is used rather than univariate z-score thresholds because it accounts for correlations between variables and identifies multivariate outliers that would not be flagged by examining each variable independently. The chi-square threshold at alpha=0.001 with 4 degrees of freedom provides a conservative filter.

### Bind and remove outliers
```{r}
df2 <- df2 %>%
  mutate(Maha = Maha, MahaPvalue = MahaPvalue)

outliers  <- which(df2$MahaPvalue < 0.001)
df_clean  <- df2[-outliers, ]
cat("Observations removed:", length(outliers), "\n")
cat("Observations retained:", nrow(df_clean), "\n")
```

### Outlier visualisation
```{r}
cutoff <- qchisq(0.999, df = k_vars)

plot(df2$Maha,
     pch  = 19, cex = 0.5,
     col  = ifelse(df2$Maha > cutoff, "red", "steelblue"),
     ylab = "Mahalanobis Distance",
     xlab = "Observation Index",
     main = "Mahalanobis Distance — Outlier Detection")

abline(h = cutoff, col = "darkred", lwd = 2, lty = 2)

legend("topright",
       legend = c("Normal", "Outlier", "Chi-sq cutoff (alpha=0.001)"),
       col    = c("steelblue", "red", "darkred"),
       pch    = c(19, 19, NA),
       lty    = c(NA, NA, 2),
       lwd    = c(NA, NA, 2))
```

### Correlation check (suitability for clustering)
```{r}
cor_matrix <- cor(df_clean[, c("grade_num", "annual_inc_log", "dti", "revol_util")])
round(cor_matrix, 2)
lowerCor(df_clean[, c("grade_num", "annual_inc_log", "dti", "revol_util")])
```
The highest pairwise correlation is 0.40 between grade and revolving utilisation, which is borderline but acceptable as the two variables capture conceptually distinct dimensions — creditworthiness assessment versus active credit usage behaviour. All remaining correlations are below 0.30, confirming that the variables contribute sufficiently independent information to the clustering.

### Standardisation
```{r}
X <- scale(df_clean[, c("grade_num", "annual_inc_log", "dti", "revol_util")])
headTail(X)
```
Standardisation (z-score) is applied so that variables with larger numeric ranges (e.g. annual_inc_log) do not dominate Euclidean distance calculations over variables with smaller ranges (e.g. dti). All four variables contribute equally to the distance metric after scaling.

### Hierarchical clustering 
```{r}
set.seed(123)
sample_idx  <- sample(1:nrow(X), 2000)
sample_data <- X[sample_idx, ]

distance_mat <- dist(sample_data, method = "euclidean")
hc           <- hclust(distance_mat, method = "ward.D2")

plot(hc, labels = FALSE,
     main = "Cluster Dendrogram",
     xlab = "",
     sub  = "",
     ylab = "Height")
```

Ward's D2 linkage was chosen because it minimises the total within-cluster variance at each merge step, producing compact and roughly equal-sized clusters. This is preferable to single or complete linkage for borrower segmentation, where interpretable, well-separated groups are the goal. The dendrogram reveals two primary branches that further subdivide, suggesting 3–4 meaningful clusters. This informed the quantitative selection below.

### Elbow method (selecting number of clusters)
```{r}
set.seed(123)
wcss_hclust <- function(k, hc, X) {
  cl   <- cutree(hc, k = k)
  wcss <- 0
  for (g in unique(cl)) {
    Xg   <- X[cl == g, , drop = FALSE]
    wcss <- wcss + sum(scale(Xg, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)^2)
  }
  wcss
}

Kmax <- 10
wcss <- numeric(Kmax)
for (k in 1:Kmax) {
  wcss[k] <- wcss_hclust(k, hc = hc, X = sample_data)
}

plot(1:Kmax, wcss, type = "b",
     xlab = "Number of clusters (k)",
     ylab = "Total WCSS",
     main = "Elbow Method (Hierarchical Clustering)")
```

The elbow plot shows the most noticeable reduction in the rate of WCSS decline around k=4, after which gains diminish. This points towards 4 as a reasonable cluster count.

### K-Means clustering (confirming k = 4)
```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
set.seed(123)
X_sample <- X[sample(1:nrow(X), 2000), ]

gap_km <- clusGap(
  X_sample,
  FUNcluster = kmeans,
  K.max      = 10,
  B          = 50,
  nstart     = 10
)

fviz_gap_stat(gap_km)
```

The gap statistic peaks formally at k=1 (trivial solution) and reaches a local maximum at k=4 before declining steadily through k=5 to k=10. Combined with the elbow plot and dendrogram evidence, k=4 is selected as the optimal number of clusters, offering the best balance between parsimony and within-cluster homogeneity.

```{r}
set.seed(123)
k  <- 4
km <- kmeans(X, centers = k, nstart = 25)

df_clean$cluster <- km$cluster

km
```
The k-means algorithm identified four borrower segments with reasonably balanced cluster sizes, indicating meaningful segmentation of the dataset. The cluster centres (standardised means) suggest clear differences in financial profiles, with some groups characterised by higher income and lower leverage, while others exhibit poorer credit grades, higher debt burdens, or greater credit utilisation. These patterns indicate distinct levels of borrower risk and repayment capacity. The clustering solution explains approximately 47% of the total variation in the data, suggesting that the model captures substantial structural differences in borrower characteristics while retaining natural heterogeneity within segments.

## 2.2 Cluster Interpretation

### Cluster profile summary
```{r}
cluster_profile <- df_clean %>%
  group_by(cluster) %>%
  summarise(
    n            = n(),
    mean_income  = mean(annual_inc),
    mean_dti     = mean(dti),
    mean_util    = mean(revol_util),
    mean_grade   = mean(as.numeric(grade)),   # lower = better grade
    default_rate = mean(loan_is_bad)
  ) %>%
  arrange(cluster)

cluster_profile
```
| Cluster | Borrower Profile                          | Financial Characteristics                                                                                             | Risk Level       |
| ------- | ----------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------- |
| **1**   | High-income active credit users           | Highest average income, moderate debt-to-income ratio, but high credit utilisation indicating frequent credit usage   | Medium risk      |
| **2**   | Highly leveraged risk-prone borrowers     | Moderate income, poorer loan grades, highest credit utilisation and relatively high leverage                          | High risk        |
| **3**   | Financially stable conservative borrowers | Moderate income, lowest debt-to-income ratio and very low credit utilisation, indicating cautious borrowing behaviour | Low risk         |
| **4**   | Financially constrained borrowers         | Lowest income levels combined with the highest debt burden and moderate credit utilisation                            | Medium–high risk |
.

### Cluster profile visualisation
```{r}
df_clean %>%
  group_by(cluster) %>%
  summarise(
    Income      = mean(annual_inc) / 1000,
    DTI         = mean(dti),
    Utilisation = mean(revol_util),
    Default_pct = mean(loan_is_bad) * 100
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(-cluster, names_to = "Metric", values_to = "Value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(cluster), y = Value, fill = factor(cluster))) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ Metric, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Cluster Profiles — Key Metrics",
    x     = "Cluster",
    y     = "Mean Value"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 2.3 Policy Performance by Cluster
```{r}
policy_by_cluster <- df_clean %>%
  group_by(cluster) %>%
  summarise(
    n            = n(),
    approval_A   = mean(approve_A),
    approval_B   = mean(approve_B),
    approval_increase_pct = ((mean(approve_B) - mean(approve_A)) / 
                              (mean(approve_A) + 1e-9)) * 100,
    default_rate = mean(loan_is_bad)
  ) %>%
  arrange(cluster)

policy_by_cluster
```
At the aggregate level, Policy B increases approval rates and is therefore expected to improve portfolio profitability. However, cluster-level analysis reveals that this gain is unevenly distributed across borrower risk segments.

The largest marginal approval expansion occurs in Cluster 4, where approval rates increase from 4.1% to 20.3%. This segment also exhibits a relatively high default rate (17.6%), indicating that Policy B introduces incremental credit risk concentrated within this group.

In contrast, Cluster 3 already has high approval rates under Policy A and relatively low default risk (10.6%). The further increase in approvals under Policy B therefore contributes profitable lending volume with limited additional risk.

Importantly, both policies continue to reject nearly all applicants in Cluster 2, which has the highest default rate (25.8%). This suggests that existing grade, income and utilisation controls remain effective risk-screening mechanisms even when DTI thresholds are relaxed.

Overall, Policy B should be implemented due to its profitability benefits, but risk management should prioritise enhanced monitoring of Cluster 4 borrowers approved only under Policy B.
